correctness.rationale: The convolution matrix has constant absolute row and column sum, attained respectively by aligning the input phases with one row and by a point mass. At nonzero arguments the raw kernel consists of four quartic periods, each repeated (p−1)/4 times. Since −1 is in the opposite coset, the periods pair by conjugation. The quadratic Gauss sum gives real parts (√p−1)/4 and (−√p−1)/4, neither zero. For J(χ,χ), the x↔1−x pairing has an even number (p−5)/4 of real nonfixed pairs and fixed term −1, so Re J≡−1 mod 4; its Gaussian norm p then gives Re J=−a. Taking real parts in τ(χ)²=√p J and using |τ(χ)|²=p gives the two asserted squared moduli U_p/16 and V_p/16; expanding the square roots uniformly gives the stated asymptotic. RESULT.md line 28 should allow either imaginary sign (p=5, g=2 gives J=−1−2i); choosing the conjugate quartic character if needed fixes the convention without changing any claim, since only the real part is used. The nonvanishing and the two triangle equality conditions give exactly the stated complex ℓ∞ extremizers. For clarity on the indirect ℓ¹ comment: two distinct occupied input sites would force K(t)/|K(t)| to be an additive character, by proportional translated phases and primeness. Then the spectrum H would be symmetric about that character's frequency. For |H|>1, summing H gives zero, forcing the center to be zero, contrary to −1∉H; hence only point masses attain ℓ¹ there. At p=5 the kernel is a single character and the ℓ¹ extremizers are that modulation of nonnegative inputs up to global phase. A fresh nine-prime raw-kernel check, including ± values of a, matched the norm and attainment; this is floating-point corroboration, not the proof.
residual_risks: No result for the real quartic regime, composite conductors, or intermediate operator norms; the arbitrary-character imaginary sign in the written proof must not be used as an identity.
